analytic.title: Affective Antecedents and Consequences of Revealing and Concealing a Lesbian, Gay, or Bisexual Identity

p.s: Individuals with concealable stigmas . . .
face considerable stressors.

These include having to make decisions to disclose one's hidden status, anxiously anticipating the possibility of being found out, being isolated from similarly stigmatized others, and being detached from one's true self . . .
The ambiguity of social situations combined with the threat of potential discovery makes possessing a concealable stigma a difficult predicament for many individuals.
- Pachankis, 2007, p. 328 This brief description highlights a set of challenges lesbian, gay, and bisexual (LGB) people face.
Indeed, being LGB often involves ongoing disclosure decisions, fears of being "outed," difficulty identifying and accessing support networks, and ambivalence in selfviews (Ragins, 2008).
Evidence confirms that LGB people make everyday decisions about "to whom, how, when, and where" (Goffman, 1963, p. 44) to reveal or conceal their identity (King, Mohr, Peddie, Jones, & Kendra, 2017).

These identity management decisions are driven by a range of contextual and individual factors (Clair, Beatty, & Maclean, 2005) and can have profound effects on relationships and well-being (Barreto, Ellemers, & Banal, 2006;Chaudoir & Fisher, 2010;Laurenceau, Barrett, & Rovine, 2005).

Fear of discovery is emphasized often and for good reason in studies of LGB workers, given the real potential for anti-LGB prejudice and discrimination in the workplace (Ragins, Singh, & Cornwell, 2007).
Deciding to reveal or conceal a stigmatized identity is often an emotional experience, yet the affective dimensions of identity management have rarely been empirically examined.
Affect could function as both an antecedent and a consequence of LGB identity management.

For example, a gay man who is about to start his first day of work may feel heightened anxiety about the desire to create a good impression, which may drive his decision to reveal or conceal his identity.
His attempt to hide his identity at work, conversely, may itself create anxiety by encouraging him to monitor his behavior and be vigilant for signs that his concealment attempts may be discovered.

This reciprocal influence between affect and disclosure decisions is featured in models of identity management experiences proposed for people with concealable stigmata (Chaudoir & Fisher, 2010;Pachankis, 2007).

There is little research, however, about how affect influences and is influenced by the process of identity management, despite the central role of positive and negative affect in individual well-being (Diener, Suh, Lucas, & Smith, 1999).
In the present study, we examine the potential interplay between affect and identity management in the everyday workplace experiences of LGB newcomer workers (see Figure 1).

Workplace studies of identity management have provided evidence of links between global identity management strategies and general wellbeing, work satisfaction, and work behavior (e.g., Brenner, Lyons, & Fassinger, 2010;Chrobot-Mason, Button, & DiClementi, 2001).

Such research, though valuable, neglects the dynamic aspects of identity management, that is, the process that each worker actively navigates from day to day, across diverse relationships and work experiences.
The current study addresses this gap by using experience sampling methods to examine LGB workers' use of identity management strategies in specific workplace interactions over a 3-week period.
This approach allowed us to examine the affective antecedents and consequences of specific identity management events, and minimize the impact of retrospective memory bias on findings.
We make several meaningful contributions to understanding identity management in the workplace.
First and foremost, we integrate affective events theory and identity management (IM) theories by examining IM episodes as affective workplace experiences.
This approach brings needed attention to the role of affect in the IM process and clarifies the relevance of affective events theory to the topic of stigma management in organizations.

Second, the experience sampling design allows exploration of the temporal interplay between affect and IM, including the possibility that the emotional impact of concealing and revealing continues into the next work day.

This focus on specific episodes is consistent with the call to increase understanding of affect in organizations by studying the events that give rise to emotional reactions (Barsade & Gibson, 2007;Weiss & Cropanzano, 1996).
Finally, our unique data allowed us to test whether individual differences in Figure 1.

the IM patterns of LGB workers (specifically, global reports of outness and concealment motivation) predict their affective experience in future IM events.
In so doing, we build a bridge between previous research findings-which concern global patterns of IM-and our event-based perspective on the affective dynamics underlying IM processes.
Three different types of affect are relevant to the current study: dispositional affect, mood, and emotion.
These three types vary along the dimensions of intensity, duration, and etiology (Barsade & Gibson, 2007).
Dispositional or trait affect refers to a person's enduring tendency to experience positive and negative affect.
For example, someone who typically experiences situations as unpleasant would embody negative trait affectivity.
Thus, trait affect cannot be described as intense, as it is just a way of being.
It is a stable characteristic of a person that is thought to result from both nature (e.g., genetics) and nurture (e.g., parental and peer influence).
In contrast, moods and emotions are transient affective experiences.
They are often differentiated from one another on the basis of etiology.
People are typically unaware of the cause of their moods, whereas emotions are reactions to discrete events or stimuli in the environment (Barsade & Gibson, 2007;Beedie, Terry, & Lane, 2005).
This distinction partially explains the higher intensity and shorter duration of emotions relative to moods (Barsade & Gibson, 2007;Frijda, 1986).
The distinction also explains why emotions often are experienced as more specific phenomena than moods, as evident in the contrast between anger (specific) and a bad mood (diffuse).

Indeed, the specificity of emotional reactions to events is thought to reflect appraisals of events on a number of characteristics (e.g., pleasantness, responsibility, control, anticipated effort; Lerner & Keltner, 2000).
Two points about these affect-related variables bear mention in relation to the present study.
First, both mood (assessed before work) and emotion (assessed immediately after IM events) played leading roles in the study.

Dispositional affect, in contrast, took a back seat because of its relative stability over time, which was not aligned with our focus on within-person fluctuations in use of concealing and revealing strategies.
Second, we faced the decision of whether to investigate broad, higher order dimensions of affect (e.g., positive affect) or narrow facets of affect (e.g., vigor).

We opted to examine narrow facets, in part, given theory suggesting that identity management may impact diverse facets of emotion through different mechanisms (discussed below in our review of the literature).
The lack of research in this area makes it difficult to speculate about the mechanisms might be most salient to the IM workplace events of LGB workers.
For this reason, we believed there would be value in studying specific emotions.
This raises the question of which emotions to study.

In the present study, we considered a set of affective facets-selfassurance, vigor, anger, anxiety, fatigue-that we believed would be directly relevant to concealing and revealing processes in the workplace.
We grounded our selection of affective facets in the IM and broader stigma literatures, as well as basic affect theory.
We note that these are certainly not the only facets of affect worthy of study in relation to managing a stigmatized identity.
For example, Pachankis (2007) reviewed research indicating that concealment can give rise to emotions beyond those examined in the present study, such as guilt and sadness.

We limited our attention to a small set of affective variables for practical reasons (e.g., survey length) but believed these variables would offer a basis for a solid initial foray into the emotional landscape of identity management.
Our selection process was guided in part by our desire to represent a diversity of affective experiences.

Emotions have been characterized by a number of dimensions, including valence (pleasant vs. unpleasant), arousal, responsibility for event (self vs. other), and relation to approach versus avoidance goals (Carver & Harmon-Jones, 2009;Lerner & Keltner, 2000).
The facets of emotion we studied included differences on each of these dimensions.
This is perhaps clearest for valence, given our selection of forms of positive (self-assurance, vigor) and negative (fatigue, anxiety, anger) affect.
However, the facets also represented a range on the arousal spectrum, from low (fatigue) to moderate (selfassurance, vigor) to high (anger, anxiety; Remington, Fabrigar, & Visser, 2000).
Similarly, facets included emotions in which the responsible party is the self (self-assurance) and someone else (fear, anger).

Finally, we studied some facets believed to be associated with the approach motivational system (selfassurance, vigor, anger) and some linked to the avoidance motivational system (fear; Carver & Harmon-Jones, 2009).
In short, although we were unable to represent the full diversity of emotions, we selected five emotions that vary widely on dimensions used to characterize affect.

div.head: Theoretical Perspectives on the Affect and Identity Management Relationship

p.s: The current study examines whether affect influences and is influenced by LGB workers' use of concealing and revealing strategies.

The notion that such interplay between affect and workplace experiences might exist is hardly new and was, in fact, proposed by Weiss and Cropanzano (1996) in their exposition of affective events theory (Weiss & Cropanzano, 1996).
However, relatively little work has applied this general perspective on affective events to dynamics specific to management of a concealable stigma.

In developing our hypotheses, we drew heavily on the work of Chaudoir and Fisher (2010) and Pachankis (2007), which represented among the first comprehensive attempts to synthesize theory and empirical evidence into models of identity management.
That is, affective events theory specifies that workplace events can follow or precede affect and thus can help to frame exploration of affect in the workplace identity management process.
In the current study, we integrate these perspectives by examining identity management experiences as a particular kind of workplace event that may have affective antecedents and consequences.
Chaudoir and Fisher's (2010) disclosure process model (DPM) serves as a launching point for considering the potential interplay between affect and concealing and revealing behaviors.

Indeed, the DPM was developed as a framework for generating hypotheses about (a) when people will disclose their concealable identity, (b) when disclosure will lead to beneficial outcomes, and (c) the mechanisms that explain the effects of disclosure on outcomes.
